name: Arcturus Defense Solutions Neurostatic NS-10
description:
The Arcturus Defense Solutions NS-10 Neurostatic is a restricted-grade incapacitating aerosol agent classified by the GLMZ Security Regulation Board as a Category III compliance chemical — the highest category available to non-governmental security actors. The NS-10 delivers a synthetic carbamate nerve agent designated ADS-7c, which acts as a rapid acetylcholinesterase inhibitor targeting the peripheral nervous system's motor control pathways. Unlike organophosphate nerve agents, ADS-7c is engineered to operate at a dosage threshold that produces profound motor paralysis within 15–30 seconds of effective exposure while preserving consciousness and autonomic functions — the subject drops, cannot move voluntarily, but continues to breathe and remains aware. The incapacitation window is 18–35 minutes depending on body mass, augmentation level, and respiratory exposure depth.

The NS-10 is a pressurized canister weapon intended for deployment by trained Arcturus security operators in high-risk apprehension scenarios — specifically, situations where conventional compliance tools have failed or where the subject is augmented to a degree that renders impact weapons or conducted energy devices ineffective. The ADS-7c compound is effective against most augmented subjects, as peripheral motor neurons remain biological in virtually all cyberware configurations. The canister uses a directed-stream delivery system with a range of up to 4 meters, and the operator is required to wear a sealed respiratory mask during deployment, as secondary exposure through ambient air is possible in enclosed spaces.

The NS-10 carries a substantial lethality caveat: subjects with compromised respiratory function, certain cardiac augmentations, or pre-existing autonomic nervous system conditions may experience severe adverse reactions including respiratory depression and cardiac arrhythmia. Arcturus's own field deployment guidelines require pre-deployment medical screening of subjects where possible — a requirement widely acknowledged as operationally impractical in real security scenarios. Multiple deaths attributed to NS-10 exposure have been documented in GLMZ civil rights filings, though Arcturus has successfully contested liability in each case.
legality: Restricted — Category III compliance chemical; authorized for use only by licensed Arcturus-contracted security divisions and registered corporate security principals; individual civilian possession prohibited; government security forces operate under separate authorization framework
specifications:
Active agent: ADS-7c synthetic carbamate (peripheral AChE inhibitor)
Primary effect: profound voluntary motor paralysis
Preserved functions: consciousness, respiration, autonomic cardiac function
Onset time: 15–30 seconds post-effective exposure
Incapacitation duration: 18–35 minutes (mass/augmentation dependent)
Delivery: directed stream
Effective range: 1–4m
Operator PPE required: sealed respiratory mask (Class 2 minimum)
Antidote: atropine sulfate injection (standard Arcturus deployment kit)
Lethality risk: elevated for subjects with respiratory compromise, cardiac augmentations, autonomic disorders
Net volume: 80ml
Price: Φ2,500
tactical_use: Deployed in high-risk apprehension operations against augmented or heavily armed subjects where conventional compliance tools are assessed as insufficient. A single effective burst to the face produces onset within 15–30 seconds; the subject collapses and cannot resist physical restraint. Arcturus-trained operators carry atropine autoinjectors as part of standard deployment kit for emergency reversal if a subject shows signs of respiratory depression. The NS-10 is never deployed in crowd contexts — it is a precision, single-subject tool.
cultural_context: The NS-10 is known on the street as 'drop spray' or 'the shutdown' — its effects are so rapid and complete that witnesses describe it as watching a person simply switch off. In corporate security circles, it is spoken of with a kind of professional sobriety; operators who have used it describe the experience as unsettling regardless of the justification. Civil rights advocates call it 'chemical surrender' and have campaigned unsuccessfully for its reclassification as a prohibited weapon. Arcturus argues that it is safer than lethal alternatives for augmented subjects who cannot be stopped otherwise.
known_users: Arcturus Defense Solutions contracted security divisions
story_hooks: An NS-10 canister is recovered from a Tier 1 crime scene — someone used it on a Shelf resident who had no augmentations and no criminal record. The atropine kit is missing, and the victim spent six days in a public clinic. The canister's batch number traces to an Arcturus internal training facility that was supposedly decommissioned.
